content: Ferric oxide, also known as iron(III) oxide, is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Fe2O3. It is one of the three primary oxides of iron, alongside iron(II) oxide (FeO), which is relatively rare, and iron(II,III) oxide (Fe3O4), which naturally occurs as the mineral magnetite. Fe2O3 is commonly found in nature as the mineral hematite, which serves as the primary source of iron for the steel industry. This compound is ferromagnetic, exhibits a dark red color, and is highly reactive with acids. While ferric oxide is often referred to as rust, this term is not entirely accurate from a chemical perspective, as rust is a poorly defined material that is better described as hydrated ferric oxide. Structure of Ferric Oxide Ferric oxide (Fe2O3) exists in several polymorphic forms, with the most common being the alpha (α) and gamma (γ) phases. In these structures, iron atoms are coordinated octahedrally, meaning each iron atom is surrounded by six oxygen atoms. Alpha Phase (α-Fe2O3) The alpha phase of Fe2O3 adopts a rhombohedral structure similar to corundum (α-Al2O3) and is the most prevalent form of ferric oxide. It naturally occurs as hematite, which is extensively mined as the primary iron ore. This phase is antiferromagnetic below approximately 260 K (the Morin transition temperature) and exhibits weak ferromagnetism between 260 K and its Néel temperature of 950 K. This phase can be synthesized through thermal decomposition or precipitation in liquid-phase reactions. Gamma Phase (γ-Fe2O3) The gamma phase of Fe2O3 has a cubic structure and is metastable, meaning it can transform into the alpha phase at elevated temperatures. It naturally occurs as the mineral maghemite and is ferromagnetic. This phase is utilized in magnetic recording media, such as tapes, although ultrafine particles smaller than 10 nanometers exhibit superparamagnetic behavior. γ-Fe2O3 can be prepared by thermally dehydrating gamma iron(III) oxide-hydroxide or by carefully oxidizing iron(II,III) oxide (Fe3O4). Ultrafine particles of this phase can also be synthesized through the thermal decomposition of iron(III) oxalate. Other Phases Other less common phases of Fe2O3 include the beta (β) and epsilon (ε) phases. The β-phase has a cubic body-centered structure and is metastable, converting to the alpha phase at temperatures above 500°C. It can be synthesized by reducing hematite with carbon, pyrolyzing iron(III) chloride solutions, or thermally decomposing iron(III) sulfate. The ε-phase has a rhombic structure and exhibits magnetic properties intermediate between the alpha and gamma phases. However, isolating the pure ε-phase is challenging due to contamination with other phases. This phase can be prepared by thermally transforming the gamma phase or by oxidizing iron in an electric arc. Recent studies have identified ε-Fe2O3 in ancient Chinese Jian ceramic glazes, which may provide insights into laboratory synthesis methods. Hydrated Forms of Ferric Oxide Several hydrated forms of Fe2O3 exist. When alkali is added to solutions of soluble Fe(III) salts, a red-brown gelatinous precipitate forms, which is not Fe(OH)3 but rather Fe2O3·H2O (also written as Fe(O)OH). Other hydrated forms include lepidocrocite (γ-Fe(O)OH), which is red and found on the exterior of rusticles, and goethite, an orange form found internally in rusticles. Heating Fe2O3·H2O results in the loss of water, and further heating at 1670 K converts it to black Fe3O4 (magnetite). Fe(O)OH is soluble in acids, forming Fe3+ ions, and in concentrated alkali, Fe2O3 forms ferrate ions (FeO4^3−). Reactions of Ferric Oxide The most significant reaction involving Fe2O3 is its carbothermal reduction, which produces metallic iron for steel production. Another notable reaction is the thermite process, a highly exothermic reaction with aluminum, used for welding thick metals such as train rails. This reaction also has applications in weaponry and small-scale casting. Partial reduction of Fe2O3 with hydrogen at approximately 400°C yields magnetite (Fe3O4), a black magnetic material containing both Fe(III) and Fe(II). Fe2O3 is insoluble in water but dissolves readily in strong acids like hydrochloric and sulfuric acids, as well as in solutions containing chelating agents such as EDTA or oxalic acid. Heating Fe2O3 with other metal oxides or carbonates produces ferrates. Preparation of Ferric Oxide Ferric oxide is a product of iron oxidation and can be synthesized in the laboratory by electrolyzing a sodium bicarbonate solution with an iron anode. The resulting hydrated ferric oxide (Fe(O)OH) dehydrates at around 200°C. It can also be prepared by thermally decomposing iron(III) hydroxide at temperatures above 200°C. Applications of Ferric Oxide Iron and Steel Industry The primary application of Fe2O3 is as a raw material in the production of iron, steel, and various alloys. Polishing Finely powdered ferric oxide, known as jeweler's rouge or red rouge, is used to polish metallic jewelry and lenses. It is also historically used as a cosmetic. While it polishes more slowly than modern compounds like cerium(IV) oxide, it remains popular in optics and jewelry for the superior finish it provides. When used on gold, rouge imparts a slight stain that enhances the appearance of the finished piece. Rouge is available in various forms, including powder, paste, and solid bars. It is also used as a stropping compound to sharpen knives and other edged tools. Pigments Ferric oxide is widely used as a pigment under names such as Pigment Brown 6, Pigment Brown 7, and Pigment Red 101. Some of these pigments, like Pigment Red 101 and Pigment Brown 6, are FDA-approved for use in cosmetics. Iron oxides are also used as pigments in dental composites alongside titanium oxides. Hematite is the key component of the traditional Swedish paint color Falu red. Magnetic Recording Ferric oxide was historically the most common magnetic material used in magnetic storage media, including disks and tapes for audio, video, and data storage. However, modern magnetic storage technologies, such as hard disk drives, now use advanced thin-film materials. Photocatalysis The alpha phase of Fe2O3 (α-Fe2O3) has been extensively studied as a photoanode for water-splitting reactions in photocatalysis for over 25 years. Medicine A mixture of zinc oxide and approximately 0.5% ferric oxide is known as calamine, the active ingredient in calamine lotion, which is used to soothe skin irritation.
